title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, RESEARCH AND INNOVATION
body_text:
The Government of India has been promoting research and innovation in the fields of artificial intelligence, quantum technology, semiconductors, biotechnology and other emerging technologies through various schemes and mission mode programmes. The details of some of the major schemes/programme is as below:
S. No. Scheme/Programme Focus Area Budget Outlay Research, Development and Innovation (RDI)Fund Deep technologies including quantum computing, robotics and space; Artificial Intelligence; Biotechnology; Digital economy; Energy security and transition etc. Rs. 1.0 lakh crore National Quantum Mission (NQM) Quantum Computing, Quantum Communication, Quantum Sensing & Metrology, Quantum Materials & Devices Rs. 6,003.65 crore National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS) Artificial Intelligence, Quantum Technologies, Robotics, Cybersecurity and other emerging technologies Rs. 3,660 crore Biotechnology Research Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development (Bio-RIDE) Biotechnology, Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry etc. Rs. 9,197 crore India AI Mission Artificial Intelligence Rs. 10,371.92 crore India Semiconductor Mission Semiconductor fabrication, packaging, design and semiconductor ecosystem Rs. 76,000 crore
Under NM-ICPS, 25 Technology Innovation Hubs (TIH) and under NQM 4 Technology Hubs (T-Hub) have been established across the country. Details are at Annexure.
As per the latest “Research and Development Statistics 2025-26” report, brought out by Department of Science and Technology (DST), the Gross Expenditure on Research and Development (GERD) as a percentage of GDP has increased from 0.64% in 2020-21 to 0.84% in 2023-24. In absolute terms, it has been consistently increasing over the years and more than tripled from Rs. 79,355.89 crore in 2013-14 to Rs. 2,44,767.81 crore in 2023-24. Further, the government is taking various steps to increase R&D expenditure, strenghten research infrastructure and retain scientific talent in the country. These include: successive increase in allocations for scientific departments; financial assistance to research institutions to carry out basic and applied research to strengthen research capacity, human resource development; and creation of state-of-the-art research infrastructure in the country. DST through schemes like Fund for Improvement of S&T Infrastructure (FIST), Promotion of University Research and Scientific Excellence (PURSE), Sophisticated Analytical Instrument Facilities (SAIF) and Sophisticated Analytical & Technical Help Institutes (SATHI) and Department of Biotechnology (DBT) through its Boost to University Interdisciplinary Life Science Departments for Education and Research (DBT-BUILDER) programme, supports research infrastructure in universities and institutions. The Government through various fellowships like National Post-Doctoral Fellowship (NPDF), Ramanujan Fellowship; INSPIRE Faculty Fellowship, Ramalingaswami Re-entry Fellowship, Biomedical Research Career Programme and MK Bhan-Young Researcher Fellowship is supporting young researchers and also attracting brilliant Indian researchers from abroad to return to India and conduct high quality research. Also, the VAIBHAV fellowship of DST provides a platform for overseas scientists including Non-Resident Indians to undertake collaborative research in Indian institutions and universities.
T he Government continues to promote greater investment in research and development through enhanced public funding, increased private sector participation, philanthropic contributions and stronger industry-academia collaboration. The key initiatives towards this include the establishment of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), the creation of the Research Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund to catalyse private investment in research and innovation and supporting policy measures.

enrichment.summary: In a written Lok Sabha reply on 12 August 2026, the Ministry of Science & Technology detailed India's major schemes promoting emerging technologies, including the RDI Fund (Rs 1 lakh crore), National Quantum Mission (Rs 6,003.65 crore), NM-ICPS (Rs 3,660 crore), Bio-RIDE (Rs 9,197 crore), India AI Mission (Rs 10,371.92 crore) and India Semiconductor Mission (Rs 76,000 crore). It also reported that Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD) as a percentage of GDP rose from 0.64% in 2020-21 to 0.84% in 2023-24, with absolute GERD tripling from Rs 79,355.89 crore (2013-14) to Rs 2,44,767.81 crore (2023-24). The reply listed 25 Technology Innovation Hubs under NM-ICPS and 4 Technology Hubs under the National Quantum Mission across various IITs and institutions, along with fellowship and infrastructure schemes supporting researchers.
enrichment.context:
India's push into deep-tech and emerging technologies reflects a strategic shift to reduce dependence on foreign technology in critical areas like semiconductors, quantum computing, and AI, which are increasingly tied to national security, economic competitiveness, and digital sovereignty. The National Quantum Mission (approved 2023) and India Semiconductor Mission (2021) are flagship 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' initiatives, while the India AI Mission (2024) aims to build sovereign AI compute capacity and datasets. The newly created Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), modelled loosely on the US NSF, seeks to catalyse research funding of Rs 50,000 crore over five years, with the RDI Fund specifically designed to leverage private sector investment via low-interest long-term financing—addressing India's historically low private R&D contribution compared to countries like the US, China, and South Korea.

Despite consistent increases, India's GERD-to-GDP ratio (0.84% in 2023-24) remains far below that of major economies such as the US (~3.5%), China (~2.4%), and Israel (~5%), a persistent concern flagged by parliamentary committees and economic surveys. The government's response combines direct funding increases, infrastructure schemes (FIST, PURSE, SATHI), and fellowship programmes (INSPIRE, Ramanujan, VAIBHAV) aimed at reversing brain drain and building a robust research ecosystem, particularly by attracting overseas Indian scientists back to domestic institutions.

prelims_questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding India's Gross Expenditure on Research and Development (GERD) as reported in the 'Research and Development Statistics 2025-26': 1. GERD as a percentage of GDP increased from 0.64% in 2020-21 to 0.84% in 2023-24. 2. In absolute terms, GERD more than tripled between 2013-14 and 2023-24. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states GERD as % of GDP rose from 0.64% (2020-21) to 0.84% (2023-24), and in absolute terms GERD grew from Rs 79,355.89 crore (2013-14) to Rs 2,44,767.81 crore (2023-24), which is more than a threefold increase. Both statements are correct.

prelims_questions.question: With reference to India's emerging technology missions, consider the following pairs: 1. National Quantum Mission — Quantum Computing, Communication, Sensing & Metrology 2. NM-ICPS — Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Cybersecurity 3. Bio-RIDE — Semiconductor fabrication and packaging. Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
prelims_questions.explanation: Bio-RIDE focuses on Biotechnology, Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry, not semiconductors; semiconductor fabrication is covered under the India Semiconductor Mission. Pairs 1 and 2 are correctly matched as per the release.

mains_questions.question: India's Gross Expenditure on Research and Development (GERD) as a percentage of GDP remains significantly lower than that of major global economies despite recent increases. Discuss the structural challenges responsible for this gap and evaluate the effectiveness of recent government initiatives such as the RDI Fund and ANRF in addressing them.

mains_questions.question: Examine the role of mission-mode programmes like the National Quantum Mission, India AI Mission, and India Semiconductor Mission in building India's technological self-reliance. What institutional and policy measures are needed to translate research investment into commercial and strategic outcomes?
